meta.title: Don Quixote of La Mancha
meta.author: Jorge Louzao Penalva (Aventuras Level 10)
meta.description: Remake de 2026 de la aventura de 1989. De momento, el mundo y los dibujos del remake: localidades, salidas, objetos, vocabulario y los gráficos. Los procesos son los de la plantilla de Rocinante.

locations.text:
DON QUIXOTE OF LA MANCHA

(c) AVENTURAS LEVEL 10

Program and graphics:
Jorge Louzao Penalva
With the help of:
Angel Louzao Penalva
Luis Gabaldón Alvarez
1989 version - 2026 remake

You are in your library. There are books of chivalry everywhere: on the shelves, on the chairs, on the floor and, above all, in your head. You sold many acres of good arable land to buy them. The only door leads east, to the hall.

You are in the hall of your house, the house of a gentleman of the sort that keeps a lance in the rack, an old buckler, and a pot with rather more beef than mutton in it. To the west is the library, to the north your bedchamber, to the east the kitchen and to the south the entrance. A narrow stair goes up to the attic.
Your bedchamber: a narrow bed, a pine chest at its foot and a barred window giving onto the street. The door leads south, to the hall.
The kitchen. A pot boils on the fire. On the wall there is a cupboard where the housekeeper keeps the food and, while she is about it, the keys of the whole house. The hall lies to the west.
The attic, full of dust and junk. In a corner, forgotten, lie the arms of your great-grandfathers. A stair goes down to the hall.
The entrance. The front door opens onto the street, to the south. To the east is the yard, and to the north the hall.
The yard of your house. Rocinante lives here, if you can call that living. To the east there is a back door that opens onto the fields. The entrance lies to the west.
The street of your village, asleep. Above you is the window of your bedchamber. The house is locked up tight. The road leaves the village to the east.

The ancient and famous plain of Montiel. The sun beats down so fiercely that it would melt your brains, if you had any left. The back door of your yard lies to the west and the road goes on to the east.
You ride almost all day without anything happening worth the telling, which drives you to despair. The road goes on to the east. In the distance, as evening falls, an inn can be seen.

Before you rises an inn. That is to say: a castle with its four towers and pinnacles of shining silver, with its drawbridge and deep moat. That is what you see. The door of the inn is to the east and, through a gap in the wall, you can reach the yard to the north. The road goes on to the south.
The inside of the inn, which you call a castle. A few tables, a bench, a smell of salt cod and cheap wine. The way out is to the west.

The inn yard. Next to a well there is a trough where the carriers water their mules. It is the perfect place to keep vigil over your arms, since the chapel, according to the castellan, has been pulled down to be built anew. The way out is to the south.
The edge of a wood. The road from the inn lies to the north. From the thicket, to the east, come faint cries, as of someone in distress.
A clearing in the wood with a great oak in the middle. The road goes on to the east and back to the west.
You come to a place where the road divides in four. You remember the crossroads where knights errant used to stop and consider which of the roads they would take.
A broad road along which comes a crowd of people: six Toledan merchants on their way to buy silk in Murcia, with their sunshades, four servants on horseback and three mule boys on foot.

You leave the village without a word of farewell, you to your niece and housekeeper, Sancho to his wife and children. Sancho rides his ass like a patriarch, with his saddlebags and his wineskin. The road goes on to the east.
Dawn on the plain of Montiel. Sancho asks you, for the third time, about the island. To the east, some enormous shapes stand out on the horizon.
You are in the middle of the plain, facing thirty or forty windmills. Or thirty or forty monstrous giants, depending on whom you ask. A road goes down to the south.

A grove of oaks where you spend the night. Sancho sleeps like a log after several visits to the wineskin. You do not close your eyes, thinking of Dulcinea, as your books require. To the east runs the road to Puerto Lápice.
The road to Puerto Lápice, which by your reckoning is a much travelled place, full of many and varied adventures. The road goes on to the east.

Toledo. The Alcaná market. You are now the second author of this history (don't ask) and you are desperately looking for the rest of the manuscript. A boy has come to sell some old notebooks and papers to a silk merchant. In the shade, a Morisco who reads Arabic is dozing.
A goatherds' camp. Round the fire, six of them are stewing salt goat meat in a cauldron. There is a lot of rosemary growing here. The road goes back to the west and on to the east.
A meadow full of fresh grass, beside which runs a gentle, cool stream. It is the hour of the siesta. The road goes on to the east.

An inn in the middle of the road. You say it is a castle; Sancho says it is an inn; the innkeeper, Juan Palomeque the Left-handed, says you will talk about the bill later. The door is to the north. The road goes on to the east.
The kitchen of the inn, with its fire and its smell of frying. A stair goes up to a garret. To the east is the yard and the way out is to the south.
A garret that, by the smell of it, has served as a hayloft for many years. There are three beds: yours, four badly planed boards on two uneven benches; a carrier's; and Sancho's, which is a mat.
The yard of the inn. A large blanket is hanging out to dry, the kind that is used for... better not think about it. The walls are not very high. The kitchen lies to the west.
A broad, dusty plain. The inn lies to the west. The road goes on to the east.
Night falls on you in the middle of the road, with no idea where to find shelter. The road goes on to the east.

A dark valley among tall trees. You can hear a great noise of water and, in time with it, some fearful blows, with a clanking of iron and chains. The night is so black that nothing can be seen. The din comes from the east.
A meadow at the foot of some rocks, where a stream drives six fulling hammers that pound a length of cloth with alternating blows. The road goes on to the east.
A highroad. It is beginning to drizzle. The road goes on to the east.
The highroad, which to the south plunges into the wilds of the Sierra Morena.
The wilds of the Sierra Morena. Crags, rockroses and not a soul. The Holy Brotherhood will not find you here. Nor will anybody else, for that matter. The way goes on to the south.
A valley hidden among the crags of the sierra. To the east a stream runs down.
At the foot of a high mountain runs a gentle stream, and the meadow is so green and lush that it gladdens the eyes. There are many trees. It is the perfect place to go mad. Well, madder.
You are travelling, shut in a cage of wooden bars on an ox cart, on the way to your village. In front go the curate and the barber, in disguise (very bad disguise). The oxen go slowly. Very slowly.
Your bedchamber. You have spent nearly a month in this bed, so dried up and withered that you look like nothing so much as a mummy. The door leads south, to the hall.

The hall of your house. On the rack, as always, there is room for a lance. To the north is your bedchamber and to the south the way out to the yard. Where the library used to be, the whitewashed wall is still there.

The yard of your house. Rocinante, who has put on a little weight this month, is feeling it in his soul. The back door, unnailed long ago, opens onto the fields to the east. The hall lies to the north.

The road to El Toboso. The two of you ride alone, unseen: you talking of Dulcinea and Sancho trembling, because he has never seen her in his life and he knows it. To the east a huddle of houses can be seen.

The great city of El Toboso, at midnight. Nothing is heard in the whole place but the barking of dogs, which deafens the ears: now and then an ass brays, pigs grunt and cats mew. To the north rises a great building; to the east a narrow lane runs off; to the south, outside the town, there is an oak grove. The road goes back to the west.
A great tower casting its shadow in the middle of the night. You were looking for a palace. This is the parish church. The square lies to the south.
A narrow, dark blind alley. There are no palaces or alcazars here, only the low houses of farm folk. The square lies to the west.
An oak grove half a league from El Toboso. It is daytime. From here you can see the town, to the north, and the road that goes on to the east.
A broad road between vineyards. The road goes back to the west, to the oak grove, and on to the east.
A dark night under some tall, shadowy trees. You have dismounted to sleep. Very close, at the foot of a tree, someone is sighing for love and tuning a lute. The road goes on to the east.
A highroad, within sight of the house of the Knight of the Green Coat, Don Diego de Miranda, who is riding with you. Along it comes a cart flying the king's flags. The road goes on to the east.

A meadow at the edge of a village, turned into a kitchen. There is a whole bullock spitted on an elm trunk, six pots as big as wine jars and mountains of white bread. It all belongs to Camacho the rich, who is getting married today. To the north, under a bower, the wedding is being held. The road goes on to the east.
A bower of trees decorated as for a feast. Here are the bride and groom, the priest and half the village. The meadow with the pots lies to the south.

The mouth of the cave of Montesinos, wide and spacious, but full of boxthorn, wild fig, brambles and briars, so thick and tangled that they completely blind and cover it. The road goes back to the west, to the wedding, and on to the east.
It is as dark as a wolf's mouth. You hang from the rope, which Sancho and the cousin are paying out little by little. You can keep going down.
A black, damp passage. The echo gives you back your own voice, calling for Dulcinea. There are galleries in every direction.
Another passage, as black as the last. Or it is the same one. There are galleries in every direction.
A hollow in one side of the cave, big enough to hold a cart with its mules. A little light comes in through some cracks. There are galleries in every direction.

A meadow, the loveliest that nature could create. In the middle of it rises a royal and splendid palace whose walls seem to be built of clear crystal. Out of its doors comes a venerable old man in a hooded cloak of purple baize: Montesinos.

An inn, which this time, by some miracle, you take for an inn. In the yard Master Pedro, a puppeteer with a patch of green taffeta covering half his face, has set up his show. On his shoulder he carries a tailless ape. The road goes on to the east.
The banks of the Ebro, with gentle, plentiful waters. By the bank, tied to the trunk of a tree, there is a small boat without oars or any other tackle. The road goes on to the east.

You are in the enchanted boat, drifting slowly downstream, without oars or sails. You say you have sailed seven or eight hundred leagues. Sancho says he can still see Rocinante and the dapple on the bank. Ahead, some great watermills stand in the middle of the river.

A green meadow at the edge of a wood, at sunset. There is a hunting party: a gallant lady on a snow-white palfrey, with a hawk on her left hand. A great lady. The road goes on to the east, to a castle.

The courtyard of the dukes' castle. This is the first time you know and believe yourself to be a real knight errant, and not an imaginary one. To the north is the great hall and to the east the garden. The road leaves to the south.

A great hall hung with very rich cloth of gold and brocade. The table is laid. The dukes are dining with a grave ecclesiastic, one of those who rule the households of princes. The courtyard lies to the south.
The castle garden, as evening falls. Fountains, mazes of myrtle and a few servants who hide their laughter very badly. The courtyard lies to the west.

The island of Barataria, which is a town of about a thousand souls, one of the best the duke owns. As for being an island, it isn't much of one: it has no sea. To the north is the courthouse, to the east the governor's palace and to the west the streets of the town.
The courtroom. They seat you in the judge's chair. On the wall there are letters saying that on such a day the lord Don Sancho Panza took possession of this island. The way out is to the south.

A room in the palace, with a royal and spotless table. Beside you, standing, is a personage with a whalebone wand in his hand: Doctor Pedro Recio de Agüero, native of Tirteafuera. To the north is your bedchamber and to the west the square.
The governor's bedchamber: a soft bed, so soft you don't trust it. The way out is to the south.
The streets of the island, at night. You are making the rounds with the steward, the secretary, the head carver and a chronicler who writes everything down. The square lies to the east.
A road half a league from the dukes' castle. On one side a deep, dark pit opens up. The castle lies to the north and the road goes on to the east, towards Barcelona.

Barcelona: the treasure house of courtesy, the shelter of strangers, the refuge of the poor, the home of the valiant. You are staying with Don Antonio Moreno, a rich and discreet gentleman, in his house. To the south is the way down to the beach.

The beach of Barcelona. You see the sea, which you had never seen before: it seems to you vast and wide, far bigger than the lakes of Ruidera. In the harbour there are galleys with pennants and streamers. The city lies to the north.
The road back to La Mancha. You ride unarmed and as a traveller; Sancho goes on foot, because the dapple carries your armour, like a trophy in reverse. The road goes on to the west.

A crossroads within sight of El Toboso. From here you can see the tower of the church you came upon that night. To the north, among olive trees, runs the road to El Toboso; to the west, the road to your village.
You find yourself before two girls: one richly dressed, like a princess; the other is a peasant. Both say they are Dulcinea del Toboso.
The edge of your village. Some boys are quarrelling on the threshing floors, and a hare runs past, fleeing from some greyhounds, and hides under the dapple. Your house is to the north.

objects.text: The iron tip of the lance.
The balsam of Fierabras (in its flask).
The helmet of Mambrino (which Sancho insists on calling a basin).

processes.source:
; Main process. DAAD runs it at the start and comes back here on RESTART.
; Describes the location (with its picture) and goes on to read commands.
> _ _
    AT arranque              ; location 0 is the title screen
    PROCESS init
> _ _
    WINDOW 0
    CLEAR fDarkF
    NOTZERO fDark          ; if flag 0 says it is dark...
    ABSENT alforjas           ; ...and there is no light (object 0)
    SET fDarkF
> _ _
    PICTURE @fPlayer       ; the location picture, if it has one
    DISPLAY @fDarkF
> _ _
    WINDOW 1
    NOTZERO fDarkF
    SYSMESS 0
> _ _
    ZERO fDarkF
    DESC @fPlayer
> _ _
    PROCESS after_describe
> _ _
    PROCESS turn

; One turn: read a phrase, count it and find what to do with it.
> _ _
    PROCESS each_turn
> _ _
    PARSE 0                ; if the phrase is not understood...
    PROCESS not_understood
    REDO
> _ _
    EQ fTurns 255
    PLUS fTurnsHi 1
    CLEAR fTurns
    SKIP 1
> _ _
    PLUS fTurns 1
> _ _
    PROCESS responses
    ISDONE                 ; if a response did something, next command
    REDO
> _ _
    MOVE fPlayer           ; if not, maybe it is a movement
    RESTART
> _ _
    NEWTEXT
    LT fVerb 14
    SYSMESS 7
    REDO
> _ _
    SYSMESS 8
    REDO

; The phrase was not understood (or the input timed out).
> _ _
    HASAT TIMEOUT
    SYSMESS 35
    DONE
> _ _
    SYSMESS 6

; After describing the location: the objects that are here.
> _ _
    NEWLINE
    ZERO fDarkF
    LISTOBJ
; Runs before every command: things that happen on their own go here.

; Responses to the player's commands. The most specific ones first.
> I _
    SYSMESS 9
    LISTAT CARRIED
    SYSMESS 10
    LISTAT WORN
    DONE
> GET ALL
    DOALL HERE
> GET _
    AUTOG
    DONE
> DROP ALL
    DOALL CARRIED
> DROP _
    AUTOD
    DONE
> REMOV ALL
    DOALL WORN
> REMOV _
    AUTOR
    DONE
> WEAR ALL
    DOALL CARRIED
> WEAR _
    AUTOW
    DONE
> LOOK _
    RESTART
> EXAMI _
    MESSAGE "You see nothing special."
    DONE
> SCORE _
    MES "You have "
    PRINT fScore
    MESSAGE " points."
    DONE
> TURNS _
    MES "You have typed "
    DPRINT fTurns
    MESSAGE " commands."
    DONE
> QUIT _
    QUIT
    END
> QUIT _
    DONE
> SAVE _
    SAVE 0
    RESTART
> LOAD _
    LOAD 0
    RESTART
> RAMSA _
    RAMSAVE
    MESSAGE "Game saved in memory."
    DONE
> RAMLO _
    RAMLOAD 255
    RESTART

; Game setup: windows, title screen and starting state.
> _ _
    WINDOW 1
    WINAT 12 0             ; text from line 12 down
    WINSIZE 12 42
    CLS
    DESC intro             ; the title screen
    ANYKEY
    CLS
    SET 255
> _ _
    MINUS 255 1            ; clear every flag except 29
    NOTEQ 255 fGFlags
    CLEAR @255
> _ _
    NOTZERO 255
    SKIP -2
> _ _
    RESET                  ; objects back to where they start
    LET fStrength 20
    LET fMaxCarr 4
    SET fCPronounNoun
    SET fCPronounAdject
    GOTO biblioteca             ; first location of the game
